NEW YORK: A broad selloff dragged US stocks lower on Monday (Nov 16) as fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO soured enthusiasm for AI stocks , raising the stakes for the chipmaker's earnings report on Tuesday and Anthropic's initial public offering later in the week. The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with the S&P 500 dropping nearly 2 per cent and the Dow falling more than 1.4 per cent. The Nasdaq suffered the steepest percentage loss, tumbling 2.5 per cent, as the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index weighed on the tech-heavy index. The SOX lost 5.3 per cent. "It's the back-and-forth in this market of the AI-related stocks catching a bid versus this rotation trade," said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. "Over the last couple of weeks, it's like a day-to-day thing where, you know, some days the AI names absolutely rip and then the very next day, you know, they're in a freefall." "There are signs underneath the surface that investors aren't panic-selling and running away from the asset class altogether, but are probing other corners of the equity market," Mayfield added.

Nvidia slid 4.1 per cent, extending its losses after Huang's resignation following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, adding to concerns over the emerging technology's rapid expansion and potential risks. Huang's departure prompted the Trump administration to issue a new rule restricting China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia ahead of US President Donald Trump's expected meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.

Related:

Trump says 'would not mind' Huang being reinstated at Nvidia

US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia

It marks an abrupt reversal of fortune for the sector. In mid-June the SOX index was up 106.6 per cent year-to-date. But that luster has faded in recent months, reducing its 2026 gain to around 43 per cent, still about four times the gains of the broader S&P 500 so far this year. That retreat helped pull the Nasdaq more than 10 per cent below its all-time closing high reached on October 6, confirming the index is in a correction. Analysts expect Nvidia to post a 90.4 per cent year-on-year earnings jump on revenue of US$109.10 billion. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.41 per cent, to 51,608.17, the S&P 500 .SPX lost 145.08 points, or 1.92 per cent, to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 626.51 points, or 2.49 per cent, to 24,509.76. WARSH REMARKS, RATE-HIKE PROBABILITY US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said on Monday that technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's latest meeting, due for release on Wednesday, could offer clues on the policy outlook ahead of next month's interest-rate decision.

Source: Reuters/fs

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration said on Monday (Nov 16) it will further restrict China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia, as US President Donald Trump began a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping. The new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres would hurt Chinese companies that use data centres in countries like Thailand and Malaysia to access advanced chips to train their artificial intelligence models . The rule h ighlights how the Commerce Department is scrambling to show it is cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive American technology. It follows reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips into China and f ai led to curb Chinese access to overseas data centres that allowed us ers to circumvent the restrictions . Trump is set to meet with Xi in China's southern city of Shenzhen on Thursday , the site of this week's APEC summit. Trump often unleashes punitive tech threats or action ag ai nst Beijing ahead of such meetings.

The rule also requires companies in Singapore, Th ai land, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licenses for advanced chips , citing the five countries as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of illegally diverting the chips to China.

Related:

Singapore assessing impact of new US chip export controls aimed at curbing China’s access

LUTNICK WITH TRUMP ON CHINA VISIT Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is among administration officials joining Trump on the trip to Asia , a White Ho us e official s ai d. Lutnick has faced intense criticism for his role in overseeing export controls on chips to China in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to an aff ai r with an executive at Singapore-based cloud company and Nvidia partner Megaspeed, which rents computing power at its data centers and has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of chips to China. Senior White Ho us e officials have disc us sed whether Lutnick should be p us hed out, Reuters reported last week. Trump , speaking to reporters as he departed the White Ho us e for the trip to the Philippines and China, said he has no plans to replace Lutnick. Asked if he still had confidence in him, he said, "Yeah, I do." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent s ai d on Friday that four government agencies had favored putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist but the Commerce Department, which was in charge, had not . His comments placed the blame on Lutnick. "It's a different viewpoint. One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China," Trump said on Monday. "They both are acceptable but they are different views." Trump also said he would not mind seeing Huang return as Nvidia CEO, adding his voice to calls for Huang's reinstatement. Megaspeed s ai d in a Nov 15 statement that it complies with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including US export control requirements.

Related:

Commentary: Jensen Huang’s downfall will accelerate US-China ‘great decoupling’

Trump says he might meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China

T IGHTER EXPORT CONTROLS Kate Koren, a former Commerce official, s ai d the rule a nnounced on Monday would have a much bigger impact on China than adding a single entity to the Commerce Department's trade blacklist, known as the "Entity List." "Nvidia and Jensen himself were key drivers of the argument for selling chips to China as a strategy," Koren s ai d. "The revelations last week put that argument into question, and the pendulum is swinging in the other direction - towards tighter export controls." The Commerce Department s ai d in a statement that the new rule was written by the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council, which also directed its release. "The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries," the statement s ai d. The rule requires overseas data centres that provide a significant volume of compute power to companies headquartered in China to obt ai n US export licenses within 90 days to continue the services or face future export restrictions. The license requirement will not apply to systems us ed by online ret ai lers and social media companies, which the department s ai d do not pose the same national security threat. The new regulation also formally rescinds a Biden-era rule that limited global access to AI chips through licensing requirements. The Commerce Department s ai d in early 2025 that it would not enforce the rule, and would rescind and replace it. But it did not take action until Monday, allowing billions of dollars' worth of restricted Nvidia chips to flow to data centres us ed by Chinese AI companies.

Source: AFP/fs

FRANKFURT: Tesla will invest €3 billion (US$3.3 billion) in its German gigafactory, it said on Monday (Nov 16), bucking the downsizing trend among its German rivals as Elon Musk's EV maker presses ahead with ambitious expansion plans for its Cybercab model. The planned construction of an additional production facility in Gruenheide on the outskirts of Berlin could make the US company's only European site Germany's largest auto plant by capacity, overtaking Volkswagen's Wolfsburg headquarters. Tesla has emerged as one of the few growth stories in German auto manufacturing. Local heavyweights Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW are all cutting jobs and considering plant closures in the face of growing Chinese competition. Germany has not been overwhelmingly welcoming, however. Tesla has faced environmental protests against the Gruenheide plant and repeated clashes with the country's powerful manufacturing union. Questions also remain over prospects for the Cybercab model intended to underpin this latest expansion.

PRODUCTION SLATED TO BEGIN IN 2029 Tesla aims to produce up to 1 million Cybercab robotaxis annually in Gruenheide, the company said in an emailed statement to Reuters, though the model has yet to be sold anywhere at scale commercially. The company said it would submit a building permit application for the Gruenheide project before the end of the year. Construction is scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027, with production set to start in 2029. Tesla said it would create more jobs at Gruenheide, with several hundred new workers sought for the first step of construction and production planning. While acknowledging the project as much-needed positive news for the German car industry, automotive sector analyst Matthias Schmidt said questions remain. "Germany should ask how much of that investment will result in sustainable, long-term employment, and how much will be automated, low-labour work moving forward?" he said .

Visitors view a Tesla Cybertruck electric car on display at the Everything Electric North show in Harrogate, Britain May 8, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Temilade Adelaja)

CYBERTRUCK MAKES WAY FOR CYBERCAB Opened in March 2022, Tesla 's Gruenheide factory was built in a fraction of the time typically required for major industrial projects in Germany, overcoming environmental challenges and permitting hurdles. However, local management has repeatedly clashed with Germany's powerful IG Metall union, which has accused the company of union-busting tactics. Tesla says IG Metall is serving its own interests. In recent months, Tesla has ramped up production of its Model Y mid-sized SUV at the site and hired more than 2,000 new employees. It is also aiming to launch battery cell production at the factory from the middle of next year. Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Austin factory in Texas at the end of summer 2027, which Musk said should make way for more Cybercabs.

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Monday (Nov 16) he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China this week, an announcement that could dramatically reshape his trip through East Asia . The president met the North Korean leader several times during his 2017-2021 first term in unprecedented direct diplomacy that failed to persuade Kim to give up his nuclear weapons. Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in another meeting during his current term, but also previously previewed meetings with Kim that never took place, including during a trip to Asia last year. Senior US officials have previously said he has no immediate plans for another meeting, while North Korea has said it sees no need for talks at this time and denounced hostile US policies.

Trump told reporters while departing the White House en route to the Philippines and China that any meeting would occur in China, and that the North Korean leader's presence was ultimately up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. "(Xi) was here ... and we're also going to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said. "So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot." Trump added in reference to Kim: "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi." North Korea's mission to the United Nations did not respond to a request for comment on Trump's remarks. The Kremlin said on Monday a planned meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi on the sidelines of this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in China would have a major impact on global affairs. Trump said he would discuss denuclearisation, Iran and Ukraine with Xi and Putin, as well as trade and the economy, but US officials and analysts have played down the possibility of a meaningful agreement emerging. Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying later on Monday that Putin could meet Kim if he comes to China.

Related:

Snap Insight: US midterms – what an angry ‘lame duck’ president could mean for Asia

North Korea signals little appetite for renewed US dialogue

North Korea has sent about 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia's war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion. Victor Cha, head of the Korea program at Washington's Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank, said Trump's comments made clear he had asked Xi to bring Kim to China for a meeting. "One could see a huge diplomatic victory for Kim if he were to share a stage with the US, Russia, China ... the three other nuclear powers in Asia - in addition to any bilateral with Trump," he said. "The common narrative is that China would not want to distract from their hosting APEC but I think Xi’s global diplomacy offensive would probably be enhanced, in his mind, if he were bringing together all of the leaders for this extraordinary meeting," Cha said. Trump's interest in renewed engagement with Kim comes seven years after their last summit ended without agreement when they failed to bridge differences over North Korea's nuclear weapons and sanctions relief. Since then, North Korea has significantly expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities while strengthening ties with Russia and China, and any willingness by Trump to make major concessions to Pyongyang risks creating friction with regional allies. Trump has referred to North Korea as a nuclear power, a status allies in the region and the West have refused to recognise despite the dozens of nuclear warheads experts believe Pyongyang has built.

Source: Reuters/fs/ec

FAST

British actor Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday (Nov 16), taking one of cinema's most coveted roles. The Bond franchise – about a British secret agent known for his charm, his tailored tuxedos and a fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" – is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. The franchise made its debut in 1962 and the movies have brought in more than US$7 billion in global ticket sales since Sean Connery brought Agent 007 to the big screen in Dr No. More than two dozen Bond films have been released. The upcoming movie will be the first Bond adventure under Amazon MGM Studios, which took creative control of the film franchise under a new joint venture with longtime rights holders Michael Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in 2025. Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the Dune trilogy and Arrival, is set to direct the new film, with a script written by Briton Steven Knight. Pattinson , who has already had a busy 2026 with films The Odyssey, The Drama and Primetime and who will also feature in Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three, to be released next month, succeeds Daniel Craig, who bowed out of the Bond role after the 2021 movie No Time To Die. "HONOUR OF A LIFETIME" "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "I'm deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team," Pattinson said, referring to producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman and executive producer Tanya Lapointe. Pattinson, 40, made his big-screen debut in Harry Potter And The Goblet Of Fire in 2005 and has gone on to star in films such as The Twilight Saga, The Lost City Of Z and Tenet. He is no stranger to following other actors to play famous characters, having taken on the lead role of the famed caped crusader in 2022 film The Batman. Pattinson only recently joined a list of reported contenders for the James Bond role that included the likes of Slow Horses actor Jack Lowden and One Night Only star Callum Turner. Villeneuve said Pattinson has "the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new". "I cannot wait to begin," the filmmaker said. The Bond series is based on novels by Ian Fleming. His first book, Casino Royale, was published in 1953. Other actors who played Bond include Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan. George Lazenby played the character in one movie, 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service. The official Instagram account of Britain's royal family welcomed the news, saying, "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond". Courtenay Valenti, head of film at Amazon MGM Studios, said: "Few films carry the kind of anticipation that comes with James Bond, and we have strived to honour the passionate fans, the legacy, and the future of this iconic character." "We are thrilled to officially welcome Robert Pattinson as our 007 and are confident he will bring something truly special to this role. Robert, Denis, Amy, David, and Tanya are embarking on an amazing adventure together."

Source: Reuters/dc/fs

MILAN: An Italian court has placed the European unit of British bank Revolut under judicial administration after finding that convicted mobsters and money launderers had funnelled illicit cash through its accounts. The one-year measure targets Lithuania-based Revolut Bank UAB, which operates in Italy through a local branch. In a 39-page ruling reviewed by Reuters, the court cited "serious deficiencies" in the lender's anti-money laundering controls. The Milan court said inadequate safeguards had enabled 24 people, either under investigation or already convicted of various crimes, to conceal financial flows totalling €41.9 million (US$46.2 million) between 2021 and 2026. During that time, rival lenders filed 265 suspicious transaction reports regarding the 24 suspects, while Revolut Bank UAB filed none, the ruling said.

Revolut is not under criminal investigation, and the oversight applies exclusively to its Italian operations, with no expected disruption to retail or commercial services. The company was not immediately available for comment. As in previous cases involving companies in sectors such as fashion and logistics, the judicial administration measure is preventive rather than punitive. It is designed to protect a company while restoring internal compliance and control systems aimed at forestalling future criminal conduct. ALLEGED SHORTCOMINGS WERE NOT ISOLATED, JUDGES SAY Milan prosecutors and the court attributed what they described as negligent conduct to the bank, alleging that it had failed to implement adequate controls to avoid illicit activity. Revolut Bank UAB, the group's licensed entity in Lithuania that operates the Italian branch, is ultimately owned by UK-based Revolut Group Holdings Ltd. Prosecutors said the Revolut group has more than 50 million customers worldwide and over 5 million in Italy, making it the country's fifth-largest banking provider by client numbers and its top foreign bank. The court said the alleged shortcomings in controls were not isolated incidents but were "embedded in a stable management model, repeatedly applied over time", which prevented authorities from identifying and freezing illicit funds. GAINING AN UNFAIR ADVANTAGE In their filing, prosecutors said the bank had been used as a "financial reservoir" for serious criminals, giving it an unfair advantage over rival institutions equipped with adequate anti-money laundering systems. The court appointed two judicial administrators tasked with broad oversight and inspection powers, which could be expanded if the bank failed to cooperate fully or if further critical issues emerged. The measure will remain in place for one year, subject to periodic reviews of its implementation. Under the ruling, Revolut must execute a 15-point remediation plan. It has five days to appoint an internal liaison officer and 60 days to submit an action plan addressing its compliance failures. The administrators are required to file a preliminary report within 30 days and a comprehensive assessment of Revolut's anti-money laundering controls within 90 days. ECONOMY MINISTRY ASSESSING POSSIBLE PENALTIES The judicial action stems from a 2024 inspection by Milan's Guardia di Finanza police into Revolut Digital Assets Europe (formerly called RT Digital Securities Cyprus), the entity that handles cryptocurrency services for European users. In a report completed in December 2024, financial police alleged more than one million violations of customer due-diligence and data-retention rules, alongside 60 failures to flag suspicious transactions. The report was sent to Italy's Economy Ministry, which is responsible for imposing administrative sanctions. The ministry has not formally opened sanction proceedings because the deadline for Revolut to file objections runs until 2027, two sources with direct knowledge of the matter said.

Source: Reuters/ec

MOSCOW: Ukraine fired hundreds of drones at Russia overnight, aiming towards Moscow and hitting a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia. The strike on the bridge appeared to inflict only minor damage, though drew an angry response from Russian-installed officials. Ukraine launched 1,336 drones in the barrage, Moscow's defence ministry said in a statement - the second-highest daily figure so far this year, according to an AFP tally of official Russian statements. The barrage came days before a summit in Shenzhen between President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. US officials say Russia's war against Ukraine is not expected to be a focus of the talks.

"The enemy has hit the Crimea bridge," Crimean's Russian-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov wrote on Telegram. "As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon." He did not say whether anyone was killed or wounded in the strike. Social media channels close to the Russian army indicated no serious damage had been sustained in the attack. The bridge has been a key target for Ukraine since Russia launched its offensive in February 2022. It has been struck several times, including an October 2022 blast in which an explosive-packed truck was detonated on the bridge, causing months of disruption. Around 600 of the drones were intercepted on approach to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. The interceptions came hours after Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian petrochemical plant, an oil refinery and a military production site. Kyiv says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Moscow's own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid -- attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. "WORLD PEACE" Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a "continuation of war". Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States had proposed Kyiv ceding some territory in exchange for being given NATO membership . Moscow has repeatedly said it will not accept Ukraine being admitted to the US-led alliance. Against that backdrop, China confirmed on Monday (Nov 16) that Xi would hold talks with Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on Nov 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The Kremlin and White House had previously confirmed the meeting. Beijing said the trio would discuss "world peace". Trump has said he intends to discuss denuclearisation and the Iran war. He is not expected to discuss Russia's war against Ukraine in the trilateral talks, according to US officials. Zelensky has warned that the Shenzhen meeting risks becoming a 21st-century version of the 1945 Yalta conference, where major powers could attempt to redraw spheres of influence without smaller countries at the table.

MANILA: The United Nations is prepared to support any denuclearisation effort that may arise from this week's summit meeting between China, Russia and the United States, UN chief Antonio Guterres said on Monday (Nov 16), despite a lack of certainty about such an outcome. "If there is a denuclearisation programme, we are ready to be fully engaged in that and contribute to make it a success," UN Secretary-General Guterres said in Manila, where he is attending a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. "This is what we would like to see," he added at a press conference. "It's not yet guaranteed that we will get there."  US President Donald Trump will raise efforts to reduce nuclear arms at a Nov 19 meeting in China with his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, the White House said last week.

Trump's four-day trip to Asia includes a stop on Tuesday in the Philippines, to meet ASEAN leaders and attend his first meeting of the Quad grouping of Indo-Pacific powers Australia, India, Japan and the US, in their first such gathering in two years. Putin, Xi and Trump are set to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. Trump's insistence that the first-of-its-kind meeting of the three leaders focus on nuclear arms reductions has riled Beijing, which has for years resisted direct engagement with Washington about its nuclear programme. China has said it was more appropriate for Russia and the US to speak directly because of their large arsenals. The UN has long advocated nuclear disarmament, warning that rising geopolitical tension and growing rivalry among major powers have fuelled global nuclear risks. Guterres also reiterated the UN's call for a diplomatic solution to end the US-Israeli war against Iran, which Trump is also expected to raise at the summit.   "What we need in relation to the situation in the Middle East, and in particular in relation to Iran and the United States, is a serious diplomatic process of negotiation to end this neither peace nor war that you are living in with devastating consequences to the global economy," he added.

SYDNEY: Helen Haines, the Australian lawmaker who lost her legs after being repeatedly struck by a car in an attack, said on Monday (Nov 16) she had been discharged from hospital and was now focused on rehabilitation. "This is a really positive moment," Haines said in her first public statement since the Oct 19 attack, adding that she appreciated the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages she had received from people throughout Australia and around the world. "They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing." Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital after being rammed by a car outside her office in the small town of Wangaratta in the state of Victoria last month. Surgeons amputated both of her legs.

Brendan Nugent, a resident of the town of Tarrawingee within Haines' electorate, has been charged with three offences over the incident : dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official. During a court appearance in October, the accused's lawyer said his client had some mental health concerns and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. Haines, an independent lawmaker, was elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in 2022 and 2025. Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee or attending community events with relatively little security. However, concerns about politicians' safety have grown in recent years amid rising polarisation, online abuse and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterised Australian politics.
